message.reasoning:
I want to write thorough JUnit 4 tests for the Caverphone class, covering all algorithm branches plus known Caverphone 2.0 test vectors like "Thompson" mapping to "TMPSN11111" and "Peter" to "PTA1111111".

I'm second-guessing my recollection of the exact expected outputs though, since I can't run code to verify them. Rather than relying on memory for these test vectors, I should manually trace through the algorithm's transformation rules step by step for each chosen input to derive the correct expected outputs myself.

I recognize this as the Caverphone class implementing the 2.0 algorithm but confusingly named without the "2" suffix. I'm trying to recall the official test data from cavtest.txt but can't be fully certain of exact outputs, so I should avoid hardcoding unverified strings and instead derive test cases manually where I can confirm the algorithm's behavior.

I'm working through "Thompson" step by step through the transformation rules — lowercasing, stripping non-letters, checking prefix substitutions, and applying the sequence of letter replacements to see what the code would actually produce.

Still applying the letter-run capitalization rules... continuing through s, t, p, m, n runs to get "Th3MPS3N", then checking the w3 pattern next.

For h I find a match and replace with 2, giving "T23MPS3N", while r and l patterns don't apply here. Then in the removal step I strip all the 2 characters, leaving "T3MPS3N", and check whether the string ends in 3 to apply the final substitution.

I remove all remaining 3s to get "TMPSN", then append the ten-character "1111111111" suffix, giving "TMPSN1111111111", and truncating to 10 characters yields "TMPSN11111" — matching what I remembered for "Thompson", confirming the algorithm is right.

Now I trace through "Peter" the same way: lowercased and cleaned it stays "peter" since it has no non-alpha characters, and since it ends in 'r' rather than 'e' the final-e removal rule doesn't apply, so it remains unchanged for now.

Working through the substitution rules, none of the consonant-cluster replacements (c, q, x, v, dg, ph, sh, z, etc.) apply to "peter", and there's no leading vowel to capitalize. Vowels convert to 3s giving "p3t3r", then the single-letter doubling rules for t and p convert those consonants to uppercase T and P, producing "P3T3r". The r-at-end rule then fires, turning trailing r into 3, giving "P3T33", and I'm now checking the final cleanup rules like stripping trailing 3s into an A.

After the trailing-3 rule converts the last character to A and the remaining 3 is stripped, "P3T3A" simplifies to "PTA", then padding with 1's and truncating to ten characters yields "PTA1111111", matching the expected memory result for "Peter". Now I'm testing "cough" as another case: it survives the non-alpha and trailing-e stripping untouched, then matches the special ^cough pattern outright, transforming the whole word into "cou2f", and I'm continuing to check whether any other prefix rules or replacement patterns like cq, ci, ce, cy, or tch apply afterward.

After removing remaining 3's I get "KF", then appending the trailing 1's and truncating to 10 characters gives "KF11111111" for "cough". Now I want to verify additional test cases too: empty string, null input, encoding a non-string object which should throw an exception, and checking that encode(String) matches the caverphone equality method.

I'm also working through the "^mb" rule by trying an input like "mbob" - lowercasing it, checking for trailing "e" removal, and running through the starting substitution options like "^gn" to see which apply.

Continuing to trace "mbob" through the transformation rules step by step: the "^mb" rule matches and converts it to "m2ob", then subsequent replacements like b→p and vowel→3 apply, then the consonant-doubling rules (m+, p+ becoming capitalized), working toward the final soundex-like code.

Then I'm tracing a second test case, "gnat," through the same pipeline: the "^gn" rule converts it to "2nat", vowel replacement turns "a" into "3", and the consonant capitalization rules apply to produce something like "N3T" before the trailing digit removal step finishes the encoding.

Stepping back, I realize this code has almost no actual branching logic — it's just a long sequence of unconditional regex replacements. The only real branch points are the null/empty check at the start of the method and the instanceof check in the encode(Object) wrapper, so my branch coverage testing should focus specifically on hitting both sides of those two conditions rather than exhaustively testing every regex substitution rule.

I'm mapping out the full test matrix: null input, empty string, and normal strings for the first branch; String vs non-String objects for the instanceof check; plus delegation from encode(String), the isCaverphoneEqual true/false cases, and edge cases like all-non-letter input where stripping leaves an empty result after the initial checks have already passed.

Tracing through single-character input like "a" step by step, I notice the vowel-start substitution creates an uppercase letter that then fails to match the later lowercase vowel class due to Java's case-sensitive regex, so subsequent substitutions pass through untouched -- worth capturing as its own edge case in the tests.

Then working through "low" as a test case, tracing each rule: lowercasing, vowel substitution turns "low" into "l3w", and the trailing-w rule fires because it ends in w, converting it to "l33". I'm now checking whether the resulting string matches the l3 pattern for the next substitution.

Continuing the trace, "l33" becomes "L33" via the l3 rule, then the trailing-3 removal and general 3-removal collapse it down to "LA", which after padding gives "LA11111111" -- a good test case covering both the w$ and l3 branches together. I want another case to exercise the wh3 branch, so I'm starting to trace "whale" through the same lowercase-and-strip-trailing-e preprocessing steps.

Continuing through the remaining rules, "l$"->3, then removing 2's and 3's, finally appending "1111111111" and truncating to 10 characters gives "WA11111111" for "whale". This manual trace is getting error-prone with so many chained substitutions, so I'm considering simplifying the number of complex derived cases to reduce mistakes.

I'll trust "Thompson" and "Peter" as known reference values, and I've verified "cough" carefully too, since the algorithm's special-casing of cough/rough/tough should make it end in an F sound, and "KF11111111" fits that intent. Given how easy it is to make a manual error, I want to double-check "mbob", "gnat", "low", "whale", and "a" once more before trusting them, since wrong expected outputs would produce misleading test failures.

Now I'm going through the caverphone algorithm's full sequence of transformation rules step by step, listing every substitution in exact order — lowercasing, stripping non-letters, trimming trailing 'e', the special word-initial replacements for cough/rough/tough/enough/trough, consonant cluster substitutions (gn, mb, cq, tch, dg, sh, etc.), letter-to-letter conversions (c→k, q→k, x→k, v→f, d→t, b→p, z→s, j→y), vowel handling (initial vowel to A, other vowels to 3, y-related rules), then the gh/g rules, consonant doubling collapse for s/t/p/k/f/m/n, w/h/r/l end-of-word and general substitutions, and finally cleanup of the placeholder digits and trailing 3s into A or empty string — so I can manually trace each of the tricky words through this pipeline without missing a step.

Working through "mbob" manually now, applying each rule number in sequence: it stays unchanged through lowercasing and non-letter removal, the ^mb rule converts the start to m2, then b→p makes it m2op, the vowel rule turns o into 3 giving m23p, then p+→P and m+→M push it toward M23P, with no matches triggering the s/t/k/f/n doubling rules or the w/wh rules since those letters aren't present.

Continuing through the remaining rules for "mbob": h, r, and l rules don't apply since those letters are absent, but rule 56 strips the 2 leaving M3P, then rule 58 strips the 3 leaving MP, and after appending the padding string and truncating to 10 characters I get MP11111111 as the final result.

Now I'm tracing "gnat" through the same rule set — the ^gn rule fires first turning it into 2nat, then the vowel substitution changes a to 3 giving 2n3t, and I'm checking through the c/q/x/v/d/b/sh/z rules to confirm none of them match before moving to the g→k rule.

Continuing through the remaining rules for "low": applying the l3->L3 transform gives "L33", then the final rule replacing a trailing "3" with "A" produces "L3A", with the last remaining "3" set to be removed next.

Then I move to processing "whale": lowercasing, stripping non-alpha, dropping the trailing "e" to get "whal", checking prefix and cluster rules (none match), converting the vowel "a" into "3" to get "wh3l", and running through the remaining substitution checks like "gh", "j", "w3", and "wh3" pattern matches to see which apply.

Continuing the transformation, "wh3" becomes "Wh3l", then lowercase "h" turns into "2" giving "W23l", the trailing "l" converts to "3" producing "W233", the stray "2" gets removed leaving "W33", and finally the trailing "3" becomes "A" for a result of "W3A".

Then the remaining "3" gets stripped to "WA", padded with ones to "WA1111111111", and truncated to ten characters as "WA11111111". Checking "a" separately: it starts as a single vowel matching the start-of-string rule, converting to "A", and no further patterns apply since everything left is uppercase and the rules are case-sensitive lowercase literals. After appending ones and truncating to ten characters, "a" resolves to "A111111111".

Testing a pure-digit input like "12345" is interesting: it passes the initial null/empty check since it has length 5, but once letters are stripped away nothing remains, so it behaves identically to an empty string and pads out to "1111111111" — a good boundary case showing digit-only input collapses the same way as truly empty input. I want to also test mixed input like "P3ter!" to see how digits and punctuation get stripped alongside the case normalization.

For case-insensitivity, encoding "PETER" should match encoding "Peter" since both lowercase to the same string before processing, giving the same result. I should add tests confirming this, plus tests for the Object-based encode method (both success and exception paths), the String-based encode method, isCaverphoneEqual, and null-handling for both encode(String) and encode(Object) with null inputs.

I realize passing a null Object to encode(Object) actually triggers the EncoderException path rather than calling caverphone(null), since `null instanceof String` evaluates to false, making the negation true and throwing the exception -- that's a subtle edge case worth testing explicitly. I also want tests for isCaverphoneEqual comparing distinct names that should differ, and comparing same names in different cases that should match.

I'm now tracing through the special-word regex branches like "cough", "gn", "mb" to check other similar branches like "rough", "tough", "enough", and "trough", since these were historically prone to duplicate-pattern bugs. I'm manually walking through the caverphone transformation of "rough" step by step, applying each regex substitution in order to verify the final encoded output matches expectations.

Finishing the trace, "rough" resolves to "RF11111111" after removing remaining 3's and appending the padding, mirroring the pattern seen with "cough" since only the first letter mapping differs. I'm now considering whether to also work through "tough", "enough", and "trough" for broader coverage, but given time constraints I'll stick with "rough" and "cough" as cross-checked examples, noting that branch coverage for this class really only concerns the actual if-statements rather than the internal mechanics of replaceAll calls.

For thoroughness in catching regex ordering bugs, I want a good spread of test cases: cough, rough, tough, gn, mb, e-removal, w$, l3/l$, wh3, r$, vowel-starting words, non-letter input, digits, mixed-case equality, null, and empty string. Tracing "tough" through the same transformation steps, I get "tou2f" after the initial substitution, then "t332f" after vowel replacement, then "T332f" after the t+ rule, and finally "T332F" after the f+ rule, with no further changes from the m+ or n+ rules.

I continue tracing through the remaining steps for "tough" — no w/h/r/l matches, then removing the "2" and "3" digits leaves "TF", and after appending padding and truncating to 10 characters I get "TF11111111". This nicely confirms that cough, rough, and tough each exercise a distinct downstream branch (c→k, r→R, t→T) stemming from the initial substitution, which is valuable for fault detection. That leads me to check "enough" and "trough" next, since I recall there's a known spec quirk about a duplicated "^enough" rule that could reveal an actual defect in Codec-1b.

Looking closer at the code itself, though, the ^enough and ^trough replacements are each mapped correctly to their own suffixed forms, so the implementation seems fine. The comment flagging "c+p error" appears to be describing an error in the original written specification (which mistakly repeats ^enough) rather than a bug in this actual code — the code already applies the correct pattern to trough.

I trace through "enough" and "trough" step by step through all the transformation rules to derive their expected encoded outputs, arriving at "ANF1111111" for enough and "TRF1111111" for trough. With these two plus my earlier derived vectors (Thompson, Peter, cough, rough, tough, gnat, mbob, low, whale, single letter "a", empty/null/numeric inputs), I now have a solid set of test cases covering the various regex branches.

I'm planning out the JUnit4 test class structure now — individual test methods for each word vector, case-insensitivity, encode(Object) with valid/invalid/null inputs throwing EncoderException, encode(String) delegation, and isCaverphoneEqual true/false cases. Writing test class...
